questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to stop feeling sad when things go wrong
Why Germans and Americans don't get on well
Why older people complain more than the young
Optimism, pessimism and what affects them
questions.why: Neil says being optimistic or pessimistic may depend more on your birthplace and age than attitude.

questions.q: How do Sam and Neil see themselves?
options: Sam's an optimist; Neil says he's a realist
Both of them are very optimistic about life
Neil is an optimist; Sam is a pessimist
Both of them are quite pessimistic
questions.why: Sam tries to see the positive side; Neil says, 'Call me a pessimist… but I'm just being realistic.'

questions.q: According to Hannah, what are Germans really like?
options: They are much happier than people think
They are more optimistic than Americans
They're careful and plan for bad things
They don't care about the future at all
questions.why: She says Germans are avid planners for negative eventualities – 'actually being cautious'.

questions.q: What has Hannah always admired about Americans?
options: They plan carefully for problems
They make everything sound better
They are very honest about bad news
They work harder than Germans do
questions.why: She says, 'I've always admired how Americans tend to be able to sugarcoat everything.'

questions.q: According to Professor Tali Sharot, how optimistic are children and teenagers?
options: Not optimistic about anything at all
Less optimistic than old people
About the same as adults in midlife
Quite optimistic about everything
questions.why: She says the optimism bias is quite high in kids and teenagers, who think 'everything's going to be fine'.

questions.q: What surprising finding does Tali Sharot describe about older people?
options: They are the most pessimistic group
Their optimism stays at rock bottom
Their optimism rises again
They stop caring about the future
questions.why: She says optimism climbs again and is quite high in the elderly, against the 'grumpy old man' image.

questions.q: According to Neil, why does optimism often fall in middle age?
options: Because of pressures from work and family
Because people start to lose their memory
Because people have too much free time
Because people move to other countries
questions.why: He says it's often because of work pressures, family responsibilities or caring for elderly parents.

questions.q: Why does Neil say he'll stay a pessimist?
options: Because pessimists live longer, healthier lives
If he expects problems, he isn't disappointed
Because most British people are pessimists
Because Sam's optimism annoys him
questions.why: He says, 'If I anticipate things going wrong I don't get disappointed when they do!'
